speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: To do so, may I ask the Clerk to distribute the handout, please?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I will also briefly touch on the other tactical considerations with regards to the Government's long-term borrowing strategy, namely interest rate levels and credit costs, servicing and repayments of the Government's borrowings as well as the development of the Singapore debt capital market.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Since Independence, the overarching guiding values of our fiscal management have been to spend within our means and to maintain a balanced Budget.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We saved whenever we could for rainy days and refrained from borrowing to pay for our expenditures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Whenever we had surpluses at the end of the term of government, we would either redistribute or endow it for specific uses such as the Pioneer Generation Fund, the Rail Infrastructure Fund, the Special Employment Credit Fund and so on.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Otherwise, we would convert the surpluses to reserves so as to grow the base, to invest and to a generate larger returns contribution in the future.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These values of prudence and discipline are also enshrined in our Constitution.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Government of the day must balance the Budget during the term of government.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The President holds the second key in the use of reserves and only up to 50% of the NIRC can be used to fund the current annual Budget spending.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There are also gross borrowing caps set by the Parliament on the issuance of Government debt securities where the proceeds can only be used for investments.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Besides these institutional safeguards, it is also vital to have alignment at the political stewardship level.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We are fortunate to have successive Ministers for Finance who are committed to the values of prudence and discipline.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Some would say that our Ministers for Finance tended to be conservative in managing the Budget.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For a small island state like Singapore, a higher safety buffer is always wise and will always serve us well.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We must always expect a major storm around the corner that could hit us and when it does, we can take comfort that we have the resources to decisively tackle and overcome the crisis.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Our prudent and disciplined management over the years has allowed Singapore to build a strong balance sheet with net zero debt and attain the highest international sovereign ratings of AAA by global rating agencies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As a result, whenever the Government taps the debt market, it is able to borrow at a risk-free rate or at zero credit costs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This opens another avenue of inexpensive funding for the Government.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In all fairness, the Government did borrow in the 1970s and 1980s to pay for the construction of Changi Airport and our MRT lines.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: However, since the 1990s, we have used the annual budget and the accumulated surpluses to pay for major infrastructure projects.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I have been pondering this topic since it was first raised in 2018; should we be concerned with this new approach and where it could lead us to?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Will these borrowings burden our future generations with high interest costs and large bullet repayments?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Or is it indeed timely to now be open to long-term debt financing so that we can achieve the optimal outcome for Singapore given the current circumstance?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Let us first look at the realities before us.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: First reality: we do have significant infrastructure expenditures in the immediate future and these are not small spending items.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Second reality: even if we were not in the midst of the COVID-19 crisis, financing such huge expenditures using current revenue or accumulated surpluses would still pose a significant strain to the annual Budget allocation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Our recurrent expenditures are already growing each year while our revenue outlook looks increasingly uncertain.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The massive pandemic-related relief spending has also exacerbated the strain on our books.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: To fund such mega long-term projects under current Budget cycles, we may have to either cut other spending or raise tax revenues – neither of which are suitable under the current environment.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, we are indeed facing a situation of tighter fiscal headroom going forward.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Should we delay these critical projects because of current budget constraints?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Well, these infrastructures are necessary to enhance our capabilities and to improve our quality of life.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Should we then just draw on our reserves to pay for these projects?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: If this is indeed the instinctive mindset, then we would really be going down a slippery slope.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We should not see the reserves as an ATM to be drawn on whenever we need money.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Reserves should only be used as a last resort such as during a devastating crisis like the one we are in today.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: They are our last line of defence and we really want a solid defence.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Each draw on our reserves also means divesting a part of our financial investments and so we will lose out on the returns from these investments and their contribution to NIRC.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Similar to the Government Securities Act (GSA) and the Local Treasury Bills Act (LTBA), we need to also hardcode the necessary prudential safeguards so that borrowings are indeed selective and controlled.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And the reason is because besides the interest cost, there is also the depreciation charge.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Under the SINGA framework, we need to capitalise the expenditure and these items – both the interest cost as well as the depreciation charge – will henceforth be an additional recurring expense item in our annual Budget.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is a significantly large expense item and will make the overall balancing of the Budget more challenging going forward.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Hence, this option of tapping the debt market to finance very large infrastructure projects can only be palatable if interest rates and costs remain low.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Indeed, interest rates are at historical lows today, presenting an opportune window for the Government to seek funding.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It also makes good sense to take advantage of our very solid credit ratings to enjoy zero credit cost borrowing in the market.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: From a capital market development standpoint, having such a high quality issuance will also deepen our bond market and attract a bigger pool of institutional investors to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This brings me to the next point on intergeneration equity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Perhaps the more enduring argument as to why we should introduce the SINGA Bill is that it helps better manage intergenerational equity when we fund very large and very long-term infrastructural projects.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: During the early years of Independence, where survivability as a nation was our foremost concern, our pioneering generations saw the need to tightened belts and save for a better tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The savings built up provided security and benefited subsequent generations who also saw as their obligation to build on past savings so as to provide a better and more secured life for the next generation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The is the self-sacrificing spirit of the Pioneer Generation as well as Merdeka Generation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: They supported the Government's prudent fiscal policy and worked hand in hand with the Government to grow the reserves and strengthen our fiscal foundation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As we built up our nest eggs over the decades, the Government would regularly share and distribute the fruits of our past successes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: At the same time, we also accumulated where we could so as to provide for higher spending needs in the future.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In 2009, the Government tweaked the reserves framework and also introduced the NIRC as another contribution to the budget to help pay for our growing current expenditures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In a way, the 50-50 sharing of the NIR represents an intergenerational balance that we want to achieve between current and future generations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Government also increased the share of Budget spending in senior facilities and major healthcare infrastructures, amongst others, to care for this generation of seniors.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: On the other hand, in order not to pass the buck of current spending to future generations, we strive to use current revenue to pay for these recurring expenditures, thereby ensuring sound and sustainable operating finances.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The financing of our large-scale long-term infrastructure with long-term borrowing is a further manifestation of that spirit of equity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Although I support the Government's greater emphasis on intergeneration equity in our fiscal management, we know it is always difficult to find that balance that everyone agrees with.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, while we can depend on frameworks like SINGA and NIRC to seek better equity, we should never discard our long-held values and ethos of always leaving something behind for our next generation and to strengthen our future.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, the SINGA Bill introduces a very important topic on intergenerational equity, that is, how to distribute fiscal resources and burdens in a more balanced way between generations?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the past, our Pioneers scrimped and saved so that future generations can have a better and more stable life, as well as more financial resources to rely on during rainy days.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It was the spirit and values of the Pioneer Generation to be thrift and to toil before enjoying.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Because of their sacrifices, Singaporeans today enjoy sizeable reserves.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is exactly because of our reserves that we can have the resources and confidence to fight the current COVID-19 crisis.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As the economy matures and demography changes, our fiscal policies and practices must change accordingly, especially in terms of the intergenerational distribution of financial resources and fiscal burdens.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: First, of course, we want to strengthen our financial foundation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We should not change this principle and practice.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But when each term of Government ponders upon what to do with the Budget surpluses and NIR, the idea of intergenerational distribution of fiscal resources should be considered.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Over the years, as our fiscal position improves, we have been able to allow this generation of Singaporeans, including our Pioneers, to enjoy the fruits of economic growth and improve their lives.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: That is why we introduced the Pioneer Generation Package and the Merdeka Generation Package and allocated more funds in each Budget to build more healthcare facilities to better look after the seniors.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The other half of the NIR must be reinvested in our reserves so that it can continue to grow.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We can then continue to have more returns to be injected into each year’s fiscal revenues to cope with the fast-growing expenditures of the future.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I think this is an acceptable and balanced intergenerational approach.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As the saying goes, "50-50, feelings will not be dissipated".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This will promote intergenerational harmony and allow each generation of Singaporeans to enjoy the fruits of our success Second, we also need to ensure that there is a balance between recurrent expenditures and revenues for each term, and that there is no deficit, so that we can sustain it for the long term.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For each generation of Singaporeans, the recurrent expenditures must be borne by the current generation and not through loans and other forms to spend the revenues of the future.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: They should not pass the fiscal burden to the future generations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is being responsible and is in line with the principle of equity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Now that the Government is introducing this new Bill, I think this is a good opportunity to adjust the intergenerational distribution of fiscal resources within an appropriate scope.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the past, we used our current Budget surplus to fund lumpy, large-scale projects.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: That is to say that, we are using the current generation's money to pay for infrastructures that will benefit future generations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But we know that as the economy matures and the population ages, our expenses will continue to increase, and our Budget will tighten.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Worse still, with the pandemic and not knowing how long it will last, our overall fiscal outlays and revenues will definitely be subjected to greater pressure.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: If we continue to use the annual Budget surplus to pay for these mega infrastructure projects, we will have to face the choice between reducing expenditures in other areas or tax hikes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Both options, given the current economic situation, are not palatable.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: With this new Bill, we can fund lumpy, long-term infrastructure projects by issuing long-term debts.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is the next best thing at this stage.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: First, the long-term interest is at a historic low so we can use this window of opportunity to reduce the borrowing cost to the lowest.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Second, by issuing long-term debt, we can achieve intergeneration equity by spreading the burden to future generations as well.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Through long-term loans, we can more appropriately spread the burden across several generations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is fair and can also avoid major budgetary fluctuations from year-to-year.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These two ceilings will help ensure that Government will not have too much debts and that it will have the ability to repay.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I believe this Bill will give the Government another fiscal management tool, so that the Government can respond more nimbly amidst the current uncertainties and have more policy space to address the issue of intergeneration equity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: (In English): Sir, I have two further clarifications.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: First, during the debate on the 2021 Budget Statement earlier this year, I had suggested that if the fiscal condition remains tight, the Government could consider special purpose borrowing to finance time-critical and worthy investments to avoid having to divest our financial investments in the past reserves.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, can I clarify whether the Government envisages that the considerations behind such one-off borrowings would be different from those of SINGA?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: My own thinking is that, when I made the suggestion during the Budget debate, it should be different.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: SINGA is meant to finance major, long-term infrastructure benefiting multiple generations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I would suggest that the one-off special purpose borrowing be to finance economic investments to emerge stronger and should only be done in the context of the exceptional circumstances presented by COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For example, we may need to invest in capabilities that take advantage of the new opportunities in the global economy arising out of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Could the Deputy Prime Minister provide an update on this?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: My second clarification is, as mentioned in my speech, one of the most invaluable international accolades that we received is —

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Excuse me, Mr Liang, you have to wrap up quite shortly, please.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is coming at a time when the country is facing another hump in its development spending needs, with plans for new rail lines, water and sewerage infrastructure as well as coastal protection measures against rising sea levels.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These important projects come amidst a tighter fiscal situation, exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The proposed SINGA will enable the Government to continue investing in nationally significant infrastructure which incur heavy upfront costs but provide long-term benefits.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: With the low interest rate environment and Singapore's AAA credit rating, the borrowing cost associated with SINGA is expected to be low.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: SINGA will make related amendments to the Financial Procedure Act to provide for capitalisation of the expenditures of these nationally significant infrastructure over the long term.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This is in contrast to the current approach of fully expensing off upfront in the annual Budget of the Government.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It will help free up cash for other needs, lessen pressure for tax increases and trade-offs on competing important investments.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: One, for the Minister to provide details on how far out capitalisation of projects under SINGA will be allowed.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Two, quantify the fiscal space created from this new accounting treatment.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Three, estimate the amount of taxes that would have had to be raised to fund such long-term expenditures, if these were made under the current annual expense approach.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: High levels of Government debt can have adverse effects on the economy, including crowding out of private sector investment, creating the expectation of future tax increases and injecting overall uncertainty into the economy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is critical that SINGA does not represent a material shift from the Government's long-held policy stance of maintaining fiscal prudence.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We must ensure that our net asset position remains strong to absorb the borrowings under SINGA.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The debt we accumulate must not put unfair pressure on future generations.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, to avoid the temptation of a "spend, spend, spend" mentality that access to "easy" money can engender, it is critical that the Government puts in place the necessary safeguards.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is important that we establish a set of robust parameters at the starting line now.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Borrowings must be carefully calibrated and we must draw a red line that should never be crossed.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I call on the Government to put in place a SINGA Evaluation Panel, to include independent expert panels, to ensure all projects funded under SINGA are highly selective, robustly assessed against the qualifying criteria provided under the Bill.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There should also be cost-benefit analyses to justify the expenditure.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is important that our borrowings are sustainable and prudent.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, Statutory Boards such as HDB, LTA and PUB have also issued bonds on financial markets to finance infrastructure projects.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How do we ensure that cumulative bond issuance, whether for SINGA or non-SINGA projects, by all Government agencies as well as contingent liabilities, remain within an acceptable range?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How will the Government ensure Singapore's AAA credit rating be preserved amidst increase borrowings?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Nevertheless, the potential interest costs of $5 billion on our annual Budget is still very significant.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This does not include the additional revenue needed to also fund annual depreciation of the capital expenditure borrowed under SINGA.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Of course, having said this, given the current low interest rate environment in the foreseeable future, I do agree with hon Member Liang Eng Hwa that it makes sense to tap the debt market now but we must remember interest rate can rise.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, this Bill does provide some buffer for interest rate cycles' yields and the potential for issuances of longer tenure bonds.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For a start, up to $19 billion in public sector green projects have been identified to be financed by green bonds, including the waste and water treatment facility at Tuas Nexus.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: SINGA has the potential to catalyse the flow of capital towards sustainable development, not just in Singapore, but in Asia.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I have seen a strong momentum amongst investors around the world towards environmental, social and governance (ESG) causes, with increasing numbers of asset owners making commitments to prioritise sustainability and investing for good in their investment portfolio.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The green bonds under SINGA are, therefore, likely to be well supported by market demand, attract more favourable pricing and have potential to deepen market liquidity for green bonds.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Last but not least, I would like to end by seeking a number of clarifications from the Minister in relation to the assets under SINGA.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: With the expectation that the infrastructure should be available for use for least 50 years, does the $90 billion limit take into account upgrading and maintenance cost over the lifespan of the infrastructure?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: If not, where in the Budget does it provide for this cost?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Two, if interest rates rise and the cost of debt servicing hits the threshold, does the Government have the right to divest the Government-owned assets in part or fully to keep within the interest rate threshold?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Mr Deputy Speaker, during the Budget 2021 and subsequent Committee of Supply debates, I suggested that our notion of infrastructure should not be limited to traditional understandings of physical structures and facilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I explained how if we wish to be a leader in the modern knowledge-driven economy of the future, we can and should direct our development expenditures ever more towards investments that are essentially weightless in nature and scale back on the lumbering, massive capital projects of yesteryear.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Today, I wish to flesh out these arguments in greater detail.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will explain how investments in human capital are not only distinct from investments in labour, but also more akin to our usual definitions of infrastructure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will also share how returns to human capital often significantly exceed those of hard infrastructure even as we are looking purely at the boost to macro-economic growth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I then offer a simple checklist of how we can distinguish between human capital investments from recurring expenditures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For starters, allow me again to applaud the Ministry for its willingness to relax its traditional reticence towards borrowing, to recognise that this really is an opportune time to exploit historically low interest rates to finance important, long-term investment opportunities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I sincerely believe that there is a pearl of wisdom in this oyster of insight.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I do have a number of concerns specific to the Bill itself.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Well, I understand that it is ultimately necessary to impose specific thresholds.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Because this strikes me as rather high given the current interest rate environment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And since rates are locked in at the time of issuance, it also raises the hurdle rate for infrastructure investments that may be considered.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Second, I note that clause 5 of the Bill also allows for monies to be raised in foreign currency, as Member Foo Mee Har has mentioned.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This suggests that if our inherent liabilities are long-term and denominated in Singapore dollars, this exposure if undertaken in foreign currency subjects the debt to a non-trivial amount of currency risk.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What mitigation mechanisms does the Ministry or MAS plan to deploy to limit such risks?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Again, while I appreciate that a duration for what constitutes significant will ultimately have to be chosen, I would note that many existing infrastructure projects would not have qualified under this rather long timespan.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Tanjong Pagar Container Terminal, for instance, began operations in 1972 and moved to Pasir Panjang in 2017, amounting to 46 years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Brani Terminal dates back to 1992 and is set to be decommissioned in 2027, by which it will have operated for 36 years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Kallang Airport lasted for 19 years and Paya Lebar Air Base, while it operated as Singapore International Airport, lasted 28 years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For public-private partnership projects, then, this would either rule out those where the Government is either unable to secure sufficient private sector buy-in which may in or of itself be a signal of the project's potential viability, or when buy-in is sufficiently large, it would preclude the Government from being able to take a minority stake.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But nevertheless, it should be clear what our trade-offs are.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Oxford English Dictionary defines it as the basic systems and facilities needed for the operation of a society or enterprise.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such systems and facilities could and typically do refer to roads, bridges, power ports or what I will refer to as hard infrastructure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Roads get us to work, power keeps us working in ports, allows us to sell the fruits of our work to markets, far and wide.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: There is no dispute that when designed and implemented well, hard infrastructure accumulated over the span of many years or decades can yield valuable payoffs to an economy and society, and, hence, is an endeavour worthy of Government investment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But it is not difficult to conceive of other systems that are critical for the successful functioning of any modern economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We sit in the House operating under the auspices of a particularly successful realisation of the Westminster system of government, without which our contracts might not be honoured, our policies not delivered or our peace not guaranteed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Our healthcare system has kept us safe from the ravages of COVID-19 and our educational system has allowed our emergence, in the words of Founding Father Lee Kuan Yew "from Third World to First".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These latter two aspects – health and education – and arguably constitute systems that enable the operation of not just our, but any 21st century economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We often refer to the accumulation of knowledge and wellness which makes us productive as human capital, and the systems that deliver human capital are essentially soft infrastructure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The recently announced American jobs plan, while billed as a US$2 trillion infrastructure stimulus, nevertheless, construes a much wider scope for what constitutes infrastructure, including the soft infrastructure components I am suggesting here.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If one is willing to apply a charitable interpretation, clause 2 of the Bill actually already allows for SINGA to encompass soft infrastructure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Part B(7) states that investments are to support or materially improve productivity and Part C requires that they benefit present and future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Human capital investments are entirely consistent with both of these sub-clauses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The only limitation being that it constrains infrastructure to any structure or building, whereas I would instead allow for structure, building or projects instead.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The standard concern that this Government has historically raised is that we should not be financing routine spending – payment of our education and healthcare professionals or funding allocated to subsidise such efforts – with long-term borrowing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But these are only recurring expenditures when viewed from the perspective of the service delivery providers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In this sense, paying our teachers, our trainers, our doctors and nurses, our scientists and researchers are certainly a variable cost.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But when viewed from the perspective of the recipients – our students, our temporarily sick, our potential inventors – we can see how we are ultimately vesting value into the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, we already systematically embed development expenditures, which by definition are deigned to be long lasting, into our annual fiscal Budgets, a recognition that what is spent on a year-to-year basis cannot be easily disentangled from multi-year projects.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: By the same token, funds devoted to soft infrastructure can and should be regarded as non-recurrent development financing, especially when returns are expected to accrue over the very long run.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My Sengkang colleague, Louis Chua, will elaborate on why this distinction between development expenditures and long-term assets may well turn out to be an artificial construct.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Another objection to Government's investment in human capital or soft infrastructure more generally is that being embedded in private individuals, investing the greatest benefits to them directly, could mean that it is difficult to justify paying for skill and experience acquisition out of the public purse.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: However, there are means by which such private returns may be recovered.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One approach is to offer scholarships that are contingent on incomes finally earned.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will return to this example in a bit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: When we think about investments, the standard approach is to compare observed returns.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is bread-and-butter work for the professional fund management industry, of which I have been a part.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One could argue, of course, that such returns are private returns and do not capture the contribution of each of these factors in macroeconomic performance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So, let us go ahead and compare their respective contributions to economic growth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Other credible estimates suggest even higher gains as much as 16%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While a comprehensive checklist for evaluating the merits of any human capital project falls well beyond the scope of this speech, I will sketch out some assessment criteria that I believe are worth considering as to whether a project should be classified as soft infrastructure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: First, as a basic principle, the assessed returns from the project should more than pay for its original outlays.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Schooling projects that permanently raise an individual's income, say, a full-ride scholarship to university, could translate into as much as 70% higher lifetime earnings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such higher incomes would mean higher tax returns over the course of the person's working life, which could easily pay for the original costs of the scholarship.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Second, most capital projects often impose static criteria, involving cash flow analysis.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The most common among these are payback period computations, which is the time needed for the project to return the original investment, in terms of cash flows generated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For hard infrastructure, these may be measured in terms of tolls or user fees; for soft infrastructure, these would be evaluated by enhanced tax revenue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Since changes in taxable incomes are not generally large, we can conceivably entertain payback periods of between 10 and 12 years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Third, capital projects also allow for dynamic criteria, such as the net present value of a project or its internal rate of return.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Such criteria are easily adjusted to accommodate human capital projects.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The main adaptation is to substitute the useful working life of a project with the average duration of a working life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In advanced economies, this duration averages 36 years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This itself would exceed the useful life threshold of 35 years that I outlined earlier for hard infrastructure projects.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This protects against unexpected changes in interest rates and the need to roll over borrowing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What might some examples of soft infrastructure projects, which broadly meet the conditions I set out above, be?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Workers' Party manifesto has also suggested raising the target percentage of university graduates per cohort, expanding additional baseline funding for less popular schools and expanding the number of infant care centres, especially in demographically-consistent neighbourhoods.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: All these examples could conceivably qualify as long-term human capital accumulation projects.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Government pays for all the costs of University or the continuing education programme, perhaps subject to a very modest co-payment as collateral.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The recipient would then pay off that acquired debt only in the event that they secure a job, following graduation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, some details, such as the specific major that is allowed to be undertaken, may need to be finessed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But the overall idea strikes me as eminently implementable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The key difference here is that these schools would be funded indirectly by the vouchers, instead of direct MOE-approved funding.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The upshot of such schools is that they may even generate excellent test scores, even if this objective does not feature in their original mandates.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In closing, allow me to also touch on why the benefits of human capital accumulation go far beyond simply improving the productive capacity of our economy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A nation rich in human capital is often one that is simultaneously rich in ideas and experiences, happiness and well-being, wisdom and understanding.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These contribute far beyond the narrow scope of economics.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: An educated and informed populace will be engaged, creative participants in our political process, enhancing our democratic credibility.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Creative and curious individuals also bring out diversity and novelty to our social environment, enriching our cultural and artistic landscape.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, Gary Becker, the Nobel Prize-winning economist who pioneered much of the early work on human capital, deeply understood the importance of habits, culture and social interactions and the role they played in the long-run success of a nation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is in this spirit, extending beyond only dollars and cents, that I am making the case for us to expand our conceptualisation of SINGA infrastructure beyond structures and buildings, to encompass investment in our children, in our people, in the one resource that we truly have as a country.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: On that note, Mr Deputy Speaker, I offer my support for the Bill.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 5.15 pm.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.53 pm until 5.15 pm. ﻿Sitting resumed at 5.15 pm.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: It has been remarked that it is efficient to issue new bonds under the proposed Significant Infrastructure Government Loan Act (SINGA) as it allows the country to benefit from the current low interest rate environment.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: To place this remark in perspective, it is helpful to recognise that for a small, open economy like Singapore that is well integrated with the international capital market, the interest rate charged on a sovereign loan is roughly speaking the sum of a safe rate of interest such as the interest on the US Treasury Bill and a credit risk.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: While the Singapore economy largely takes a safe rate of interest as given, the currently low credit risk is the result of past fiscal prudence.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Our capacity in the future to generate tax revenue to meet our future spending needs will be necessary to enable the country to maintain this low credit risk.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, the credit risk can move up or down even when the safe interest rate stays constant.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: What factors led to the creation of fiscal space in the past and what factors might affect Singapore's credit rating in the future?

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Before answering these two questions, it is good to quickly review the justification for SINGA Bill that we are talking about in Parliament.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: As I read it, there are two dimensions to the infrastructural investment.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The first is public investment, such as in roads and major highways, which serves to raise the productivity of firms.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: There is evidence that the stock of public capital – highways, roads and so on – complements private capital so that the public capital raises the returns to private business investments.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The second is infrastructural investment which serves to mitigate the adverse effects of climate change, such as seawalls and dykes.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In the absence of this second type of investment, not only would national productivity fall, lives could be at risk with coastal hazards.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Since the benefits derived can be enjoyed by as yet unborn generations, the Government of the day must act on their behalf.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: It is also justifiable to issue new bonds to finance such infrastructural investments so that future generations can share in bearing the tax burden.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: To the question of what factors led to the currently low credit risk.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: No doubt, Singapore's remarkable economic catch-ups since Independence effectively expanded the tax base at given tax rates.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: With economic growth, real income steadily increased decade after decade.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Income inequality was not a serious problem in the first couple of decades after Independence as industrialisation increased the demand for relatively unskilled to semi-skilled workers, thus pulling up their wage earnings.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: With a relatively young population then, healthcare spending was a smaller share of the Budget.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, the demand for fiscal resources to support social spending was less pressing.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Unlike unfunded social security systems, a pay-as-you-go system where current taxes on the working young are used to pay for the benefits of retirees, Singapore's fully funded social security system, the Central Provident Fund, also added to national saving.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: These factors altogether contributed to Singapore's good credit rating.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: That was how we achieved our low credit risk.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Looking to the future, what factors might affect Singapore's credit rating?

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: The concept of fiscal sustainability is useful as a way to think about how to maintain a low credit risk.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Although a country can still run into Budget deficits – when it is hit by a recession, for example – it must ultimately plan to generate tax revenue that is in excess of current spending in other years if it is to be able to service an outstanding stock of public debt.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: To use an analogy, suppose that at the start of your career, you take out a loan.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Then, although in future periods, you might still occasionally borrow, there must be sufficiently many periods during which you spend less than your income for you to be credit worthy.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In anticipation of increased social spending, in particular on health, with an ageing population, it would be necessary to raise taxes in order to remain fiscally sustainable.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: From the perspective of the analysis just provided, one benefit to the country of raising tax revenue in anticipation of higher social spending is that the credit risk or risk premium can be kept low.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, whatever the safe interest rate is, the borrowing costs incurred to service the loan undertaken in this Act can be kept relatively low by maintaining good credit worthiness.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Returning to the analogy, suppose that in the course of your working life, the interest rate unexpectedly rises.

speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
text: Then, in order for you not to default, you would have to tighten your belt and cut spending unless you discover that your income is also going to increase.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I am concerned about how we can do more to guard against burdening our future generations.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: After all, such borrowing needs to be serviced and repaid.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to be mindful as we do not have natural resources for sources of revenue, unlike other nations.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, our manpower capabilities and earning capacity are important.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must be able to weather economic ups and downs and future political and social developments.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such uncertainties could potentially derail projects – just as we are experiencing the disruptions to our construction sector caused by the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The other options are out of the question.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Commercialising public services will impose hardship on the lower income groups.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Government may still need to step in to render assistance and subsidies for the less privileged users.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It remains important that they can be self-sustaining and operationally viable.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the SINGA Bill is no indication that the Government is short of funds for national development.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Despite the drawdown for the five COVID-19 Supplementary Budgets, our total financial assets are probably still growing because large capital inflows should have allowed MAS to accumulate more foreign currency assets in order to keep the Singapore dollar within its policy band.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, SINGA is just an additional financing scheme and not an absolutely necessary funding source.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government's narrative about intergenerational equity is also not an accurate description of the SINGA scheme.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since there is no lack of fiscal resources, intergenerational equity can be achieved as long as the Government allocates the resources accordingly.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is no need to borrow to achieve intergenerational equity.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the Government's mention of intergenerational equity for the first time is heartening and I hope it will use it as a guiding principle from now on.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Up till now, the Government has always frontloaded all the infrastructural costs to the current generation of Singaporeans and, at the same time, parked a disproportionate amount of current fiscal resources into the national reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In addition, the social security costs, namely, retirement and healthcare costs of Singaporeans, are all self-funded by themselves, without burdening the future generations.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is unlike the social systems in many developed countries like Japan where a major part of the taxes collected from the current working population is used to support the retirement and healthcare spending of the older retiree generation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As a result, the current generation in Singapore has to shoulder a disproportionate amount of the infrastructure and social security costs and has to struggle with a lower level of disposable income, giving rise to the phenomenon popularised by Jack Neo's movie, "Money No Enough".

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, there is an urgent need to address this intergenerational inequity.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, SINGA is not necessarily the best way to achieve that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Rather, as I have said at the start, I support the SINGA scheme for better financial efficiency and fiscal accountability in the public finances.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Unless GIC/MAS can consistently earn a positive spread over the borrowing costs of the SINGA loans, there is no reason to borrow the SINGA loans and not make use of our current resources to fund our infrastructure projects.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It will be a big step forward for our local bond markets if the Government can issue Singapore Government Securities or bonds with longer maturities like 20 years and 30 years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For better fiscal accountability, I would expect to see the pre-investment feasibility studies for the SINGA projects to be subject to public consultation so that we can tap the collective wisdom of Singaporeans and not be guided only by the experts engaged by the Government.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Regular progress reports of SINGA projects should also be submitted to Parliament for scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   The SINGA Bill is no indication that the Government is short of funds for national development.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today, the total financial assets owned by our country have reached $1.35 trillion by end March 2020.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And despite the drawdown for the five COVID-19 Supplementary Budgets, our total financial assets are probably still growing because large capital inflows should have allowed MAS to accumulate more foreign currency assets in order to keep the Singapore dollar within its policy band.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even without touching the principal of the reserves, the Net Investment Return of about $40 billion a year from the reserves is enough to fund the infrastructural projects and social spending increases especially those in the healthcare area into the foreseeable future.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence SINGA is just an additional financing scheme and not an absolutely necessary funding source.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Because we have the sufficient resources, we do not need to use SINGA to achieve intergenerational equity, that is, allocate national resources between generations fairly.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As long as the Government recognises the huge size of our national reserves and that it continues to grow, we are already providing a strong safety net for our future generations.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is time that we do more for this present generation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I support the SINGA Bill more because it can increase our financial efficiency and fiscal accountability.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Financial efficiency means that, when the returns from the reserves are higher than the borrowing interest of international market, we should not tap on our current resources to fund significant infrastructure projects; instead, it is more worthwhile to borrow from the international financial market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: SINGA therefore, provides an additional option for the Government.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have issued more than S$700 billion Singapore-dollar bonds and treasury bills.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to do this with robust financial approaches that provide differentiated expenditure support.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As such, I find the overall principles laid out for the SINGA bonds to be sound for our long-term infrastructure investments.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Having said that, the principle of equitable sharing of expenditure holds up best if the proposed infrastructure provides clear "net" benefits to the economy and society.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This requires us to be prudent on our assessment of the infrastructure project investments' cost and benefits.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If the cost outweighs the benefits, we could burden future generations with a potential growing net debt load and this is an outcome we must avoid.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is also important to stress that SINGA, like any other forms of borrowings, needs to be repaid.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to ensure that future revenue growths can accommodate the repayments and maintain Singapore's strong balance sheet and credit ratings.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have met some residents who expressed concerns on whether we are passing on debt to future generations.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Residents have expressed that we need to be cautious and ensure we pass on assets and not liabilities to our children.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With their concerns included, I would like to make five clarifications.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Having said that, our GDP in the past had higher year-on-year growth rates.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, may I ask to what extent the limit took into account future growth trends in the coming years, especially when we are expecting a slower recovery due to both the COVID-19 context and ourselves a maturing economy?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Five, as a key principle of SINGA bonds is the equitable sharing of cost across generations, will capitalisation and depreciation be linear throughout or frontloaded to take into account higher maintenance cost in later years?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Lastly, I would suggest to include initiatives to ensure that infrastructures are built to cater for larger capacity and with better materials, methodologies and technologies.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These may translate into higher capital cost today, but can lower downstream cost expenditure for an ageing asset, adding to my previous point on avoiding putting burden on maintenance cost on future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We, however, must continue to be prudent on the deployment of these funds as the effects will ripple and reverberate into multiple generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The current proposal presents an opportunity to arbitrage – we can make more with our capital in our reserves, generating returns to fund our social programmes, as compared to the cost of borrowing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, it makes sense to borrow under these prevailing circumstances where there is low interest rate and we enjoy a good credit rating.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And in that regard, I am happy to note the Government's safeguards built into this Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I listened intently to the speech of the hon Member Assoc Prof Jamus Lim when he argued that infrastructure should be extended to not just hard infrastructure, but also soft infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And by that, he meant an investment in health, education, accumulation of knowledge and human capital.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: While I listened to him, I think there is a lot of agreement, as opposed to disagreement, on the need to invest in these areas.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In fact, if we were to reflect back on how the Government has been investing in these areas – things like SkillsFuture, building more hospitals, schools – we can see that that is also part of what the governing party is doing, investing in soft infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The focus of this Bill, however, is financing infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And this is where we need to be careful because we are talking about sending a bill to our children, our children's children to settle.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And I thought what the hon Member Prof Hoon Hian Teck said was quite compelling because he cautioned that the situation can change.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There could be a situation whereby the safe interest rate, in his words, can increase.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And this is where I think the rub lies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What are the infrastructure developments we should send to be settled by our children and our children's children?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Here, I would respectfully submit that it is safer and more prudent for us to invest in soft infrastructure as much as we can and settle the bill ourselves.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First on the nature and the structure of the bonds and, second, on the realities of implementation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, on the nature and structure of the bonds.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, I have two points to make.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, the interplay between the constitutional safeguards – and the hon Deputy Prime Minister mentioned the Reserves Protection Framework – and SINGA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My question relates to the workings of the procedure.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Say, for example, the Bill is passed and the Government intends to issue bonds.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Would the Government come back to Parliament for a resolution to be passed and would it still be subject to the discretionary approval of the President?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I respectfully seek a clarification from the Deputy Prime Minister on this matter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The second point I wish to make is in relation to our commitment to green bonds.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Today, he mentioned that one of the objectives of SINGA is to build a safe, green, liveable environment.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To further encourage sustainability efforts, would the Government be minded to stipulate at least a minimum percentage of SINGA bonds that will be green?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This will have a salutatory effect of ensuring the high percentage of infrastructural projects being undertaken in Singapore with sustainable measures in place.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On to my second point about the realities of implementation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What about projects that may, for one reason or another, be aborted?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For instance, when there is a change in government.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We cannot predict the future, but we have seen examples all over the world.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One government may come in and say it wishes to build a wall.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Closer to home, one government may say "build a high-speed railway system"; another government may decide not to do it.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Would it not be prudent to work in a requirement that the government of the day which wishes to abandon infrastructural projects funded by SINGA bonds must ensure that it is able to finance the abortive costs from its current revenue?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The logic behind this Bill is compelling, but I sense nervousness in the speeches of the hon Members, such as Mr Edward Chia, Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Ms Foo Mee Har.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And it is understandable, because borrowing always entails a risk, just as the fruits of spending are always alluring.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But I am satisfied that the safeguards that the hon Deputy Prime Minister highlighted are safeguards that will stand us in good stead.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, notwithstanding my comments, Sir, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In October last year, I shared that there is scope to rethink Singapore's position on debt, instead of funding our expenditures solely with higher cost equity funding or funding from our reserves.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is especially if the funds are being used for quality investment projects that will benefit current and future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Today’s Bill represents an important milestone for us as a country and, while it may have been a little later than some had hoped, it is, indeed, better late than never.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In finance, we often speak of an optimal capital structure for a firm – the ability to have a proportion of debt and equity that results in the lowest Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) when making the capital management decision.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While certain commentators may liken Government finances to a household budget, unlike a household, firms and countries can be assumed to last into perpetuity.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Debt is not inherently bad per se and, if it can be employed effectively to increase returns or result in a lower WACC on an overall basis, then it should always be considered as a viable option.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, while we can have a different philosophical view of what the ideal structure should be on the national level, we must be keenly aware that equity funding or funding from our reserves is not free.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I would now like to take the time to seek some clarifications on several points in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The first is on the capitalisation of expenditure on nationally significant infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Again, this is another welcome change from an alignment of accounting practices point of view.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: After all, the long useful lives of infrastructure projects do suggest that they clearly fall under the accounting definition of an asset, as it is a present economic resource that has the potential to produce economic benefits.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This change is in contrast to the current practice of charging off development expenditure annually.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is a fraction of what it would have been had we stuck to the current accounting treatment.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The second point I would like to talk about is the type of projects which have been identified for the purpose of SINGA.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: These include infrastructure intended for a list of specific purposes as listed in section 2, such as transport, water treatment, alleviation of floods and so on.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: My colleague Assoc Prof Jamus Lim has built a strong case for human capital as a form of soft infrastructure investment.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, when we look at US President Biden's $2 trillion infrastructure plan, we see that it includes a planned funding of the care economy, which includes $400 billion towards expanding access to quality, affordable home- or community-based care for the elderly and people with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It will also cover investments in schools, childcare facilities and workforce development programmes, among others.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In a knowledge-based economy, intellectual and human capital are just as important, if not more important than physical hard assets.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We should not solely be focusing on conventional property, plants and equipment as possible infrastructure projects to finance with borrowing.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As it is, intellectual property and other intangible assets can already be capitalised under a firm’s balance sheet under accounting rules, given the recognition of the economic benefits that they generate.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As a Government, we should seriously consider this as an extension of the SINGA Bill, as compared to only that of traditional infrastructure assets.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As shared by my colleague Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, many existing infrastructure projects would not have qualified under this rather long timespan.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am concerned about how practical that might be in an era where technological and environmental needs are changing so rapidly.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If climate change were, indeed, a motivating factor for the need for infrastructure changes, it would be far from accurate to assume that any infrastructure planning now will be useful for the next 50 years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Rapid technological changes have shaped the tech infrastructure needed to keep our economy competitive.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Over the past 20 years, we have moved from an era of 3G cellular networks in the 2000s, to 4G in 2010s and, finally, the rolling out of 5G networks from 2020.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: That is roughly a 10-year gap between each generation of cellular networks.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It would be extremely difficult for anyone to predict with utmost confidence if the infrastructure we are building for 5G today, for example, will continue to be relevant 10 or even 20 years down the line, let alone 50 years at a minimum.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: First constructed more than 30 years ago, the replacement of sleepers, signalling equipment, track upgrading and power supply systems over the last couple of years have meant that it is as good as replacing the entire system with a brand-new set.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even power plants, such as one of the newer CCGT plants in Singapore, only have a useful life of around 25 years.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: My fourth point covers that of green financing.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We aspire to be a green hub and we have laid out grand plans in our current Singapore Green Plan 2030.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: From my understanding, some of these projects, such as Tuas Nexus, have been identified.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As a Government, we should aspire to lead by example and set a laudable target for how much we plan to spend on green infrastructure itself.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Further, I believe that the financing of nationally significant infrastructure should be tied to the mandatory completion of rigorous environmental, heritage and social impact assessments done using the best available science at reasonable cost.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Such studies should be made fully available to the public for feedback and for the public to take any private mitigation measures if necessary.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This would then allow the full buy-in from society at large on the benefits of such infrastructure projects.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I recognise that advisory services, such as the associated design, investigative and engineering studies, surveys or, say, research, are already deemed as qualifying capital expenditure.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The key caveat here, of course, is that such advisory services have to be reasonable, relative to the total project cost.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even though I am sure there are many considerations and technical challenges to work through, it would be unwise if consultancy fees end up being 90% of the cost of the actual project, for example.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, I wonder if the Government would also include limits on how much should be spent on advisory fees, as compared to the overall construction cost of the project.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The fifth point I would like to cover looks at some of the numbers as specified within the SINGA Bill.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Debt levels, in themselves, cannot be seen in isolation and we need to assuage Singaporeans that the level of borrowing is not unsustainable.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Credit rating agencies often compare debt levels to net worth or net assets or, in the case of sovereign credit ratings, usable reserves, for example.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: My question for the Deputy Prime Minister, therefore, is how much does this $90 billion represent, relative to Singapore's current account receipts and reserves?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Further, Minister Ong Ye Kung has mentioned that we would need to spend more than $60 billion over this decade to expand and renew our rail networks while Prime Minister Lee has mentioned that Singapore is probably going to spend $100 billion, possibly more, to protect our country against rising sea levels.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I would thus like to ask the Deputy Prime Minister to put into context how is this sum of $90 billion of debt financing determined?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And if there are any quantifiable targets such as the total expected infrastructure spending in dollar terms over the next one to two decades?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And how much of the funds are already earmarked for specific projects?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: How does this compare to the current and future expected Singapore Government Securities yields that the Ministry is projecting?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Singapore's 10-year bond yields stand about 1.5% today while 30-year bond yields are about 1.9%.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Based on my checks, historical average bond yields of varying bond durations are only at about 2.5% to 2.8%, notwithstanding a wide range of less than 1% to almost 5%, 6%.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The average is significantly lower than the implied yield to maturity of 5.6%.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Lastly, with regards to the qualifying amount of capital expenditure being at least $4 billion or more, I would like to ask the Deputy Prime Minister how this number was derived as well?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In 2008, the KPE was built at a cost of $1.8 billion.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Inflation, notwithstanding, the value that the project has brought to Singaporeans has been immense, especially residents staying in the Northeast, such as that of our Sengkang residents.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In 2014, the 800-megawatt state-of-the-art power plant by PacificLight was built at a cost of $1.2 billion.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: There is also a question of whether the definition of "nationally significant infrastructure" being defined under Part I as being geographically located "in Singapore" may restrict the spending needs for infrastructure that crosses borders.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A nationally significant infrastructure, the Linggiu Reservoir, which Singapore built at a cost of more than $300 million in Malaysia comes to mind.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Further, should the Government decide to set a much more ambitious, renewable energy target, the infrastructure costs for the import of electricity, especially solar electricity from overseas, would also not fall within the purview of this SINGA Bill.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The first is that, I agree with Deputy Prime Minister Heng that there should be various strict safeguards on the projects that can qualify for borrowing and the amounts that can be borrowed.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Similarly, when it comes the use of our reserves via the NIRC, it too has strict safeguards in place.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Ultimately, any sound policy decision should have safeguards built in and, hence, if we decide to tap on Singapore's ample fiscal space to fund our investments into our people, we should not fear the slippery slope of there not being any safeguards that can be put in place.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
