text: The second is that, again, I agree with Deputy Prime Minister Heng that borrowing for nationally significant infrastructure will spread these lumpy expenditures across the generations who will benefit.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If we want to be a progressive society that firmly believes in the principles of fairness, we should also be acutely aware that the converse is also true.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We should never forget the sacrifices the earlier generations of Singaporeans have made in building this nation and must always keep this in mind.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If I may just quickly respond to Member Mr Murali who raised two points actually.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The first, he talked about financing versus investment and he stressed the point that the Government, indeed, has invested quite a bit in soft infrastructure and human capital projects.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And then, he said that the purpose of this Bill is actually for financing.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: First, my three observations, which all relate to the larger point about long-term planning.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Fundamentally, SINGA reflects this Government's commitment and orientation to plan for the long term and govern in the long-term interest of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: At the same time, SINGA has an eye on the Government's 100-year plan for our coastal defence infrastructure, to secure Singapore against the very long-term threat of rising sea levels posed by climate change.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: These long-term infrastructural plans are essential to our mission of continuing to improve the lives of Singaporeans, present and future.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Indeed, our history clearly shows how we are the current beneficiaries of long-term plans and big bets in strategic infrastructure that previous Governments had made.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: For example, plans for the first container terminal in Singapore – and the region – located at Tanjong Pagar were made way back in the 1960s, when containerisation was not yet the norm, in fact far from it.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The first vessel the Terminal received had 300 containers on board; compared to the more than 1,000 people gathered on shore to receive it.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And in fact, container volumes did not really take off, until the next decade, in the 1980s.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But finally, the long-term bet paid off, and since then, more long-term plans had been made and implemented for the Brani Terminal in the 1990s, Pasir Panjang Phase 1 and 2 in the 2000s, and Phase 3 and 4 in the last decade, such that we have the Port of Singapore that we have of today, after almost 60 years since the first plan for a container port was laid.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In short, it was a decisive bet, a far-sighted decision and a constant focus on what is next and what is on the horizon that had allowed Singapore to move ahead and stay ahead of the competition.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It was a similar story with Changi Airport.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Plans were made in the 1970s, with the aim then already to be Asia's largest airport at that time of opening.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: A significant amount of land had to be reclaimed, and Terminal 1 opened in 1981.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Plans were made in 1970s, Terminal 1 opened in 1981.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Terminal 2 then opened in the next decade, in 1991.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Followed by Terminal 3 in the decade after that, in 2008.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And of course, Terminal 4, in the following decade, in 2016.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, decade after decade, a quantum leap each time, anchored on robust long-term planning and execution.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Looking ahead, therefore, SINGA, I think, underlies this Government's continued commitment to a long-term, ambitious strategy for our national infrastructure, to secure our future and success well into SG100.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: My second observation about long-term planning is about this Government's commitment to a long-term fiscal strategy, to sustain and properly steward our strategic fiscal resources and to take full advantage of our strong fiscal standing, in the best long-term interest of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Crucially, the Government is not looking to borrow for significant infrastructure because it lacks money.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Quite the contrary, it is looking to borrow, so as to take full advantage of our fiscal strength and the expected low cost of debt capital going forward, instead of expending our existing financial resources for lumpy infrastructural outlays, when these resources could be deployed and invested to generate good returns for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In other words, the Government's strategy of borrowing for infrastructure on the one hand and investing on the other is an astute, long-term strategy to fully leverage relatively low interest rates and avoid the opportunity cost of dipping into our own resources.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The third observation I would make is this: beyond SINGA, beyond physical infrastructure, I think successive Governments have always made long-term plans and investment in our soft infrastructure, in human capital development, to ultimately improve the lives of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And it will continue be a constant work in progress but let us look at their track records.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Through the decades, successive Governments had invested steadily and decisively in education, in skilling Singaporeans, because ultimately, that is our surest way to better opportunities and better lives.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And from a focus on 15, 16 years of formal schooling, to now learning for life.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I think it is clear to see how much successive Governments had invested in education for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Successive Governments had also invested steadily in Singaporeans' health.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And of course, this Government has said that it would do even more going forward.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Successive Governments had invested billions in defence, which is in turn absolutely vital to create the basic conditions for Singapore to thrive.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: They have invested significantly in research and the building up of our base economic capabilities and they have invested significantly in our social capital to strengthen our social safety nets.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, we need to look beyond SINGA, beyond physical infrastructure, about successive Governments', including this Government's approach to long-term planning and development in general which has always been about the whole of society, the whole of nation.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The proposed cap of $90 billion in the Bill represents roughly 18% of GDP.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This is quite significant, especially if a profligate government were to take over and on this, I echo Member Murali Pillai's point about us not knowing what will happen in the future.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This lower cap would nonetheless give the Minister sufficient space to operate within the Act initially, and the Government can always come back to Parliament when there is a need for the borrowing cap to be raised beyond that.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: My second suggestion is to lower the cap for total interest payments.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The proposed cap of $5 billion in interest payments alone represents almost a quarter of our entire development outlay per year in recent years.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Given our credit rating and trends in long-term interest rates, I think this lower cap should be quite practicable.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: My third and final suggestion is to reconsider the qualifying limit of $4 billion for a nationally significant infrastructure project.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Would major healthcare infrastructure projects, for example, which usually cost around $1 billion to $2 billion each, make the cut?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: If not, why not, if we agree that the value of healthcare infrastructure, in terms of its social value, is certainly of national significance?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is especially so in Singapore where our Government is known for its long-running commitment to prudence.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But the fact that the Government has tabled the SINGA Bill is testament to a sustained commitment for fair intergenerational equity, prudent spending and an enhancement to our differentiated financing strategy beyond.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is a necessary response to an expected spike in development expenditure in the next decade to address infrastructural needs and existential threats like climate change and rising sea levels but also taking into consideration the low interest rate environment we are in for now.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is a bit different from what the hon Member from Sengkang GRC mentioned, about spending further on human capital.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It would be useful to find out from him how much more he would like to borrow on human capital, given that Singapore is already the highest ranked in the World Bank's Human Capital Index report.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Just to explain, the Human Capital Index by the World Bank measures countries best in mobilising economic and potential of its citizens.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We are already ranked highest and I think the Government has put in quite a bit already in terms of human capital.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: After all, Singapore's best resource or most important resource is our people.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I would just want to probably seek a clarification from the Member from Sengkang GRC on that point – how much does he plan to borrow for human capital.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is fair because it supports intergenerational equity.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Without borrowing, the expenses for the infrastructure would have to be shouldered by the current Government for projects that may only demonstrate their potential in decades to come.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With SINGA, the upfront development expenditure is converted into a stream of annual depreciation over the useful life of the project.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As the infrastructure is improved over the years, future generations pay directly for the enhanced benefits enjoyed.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, there is capital efficiency as we will benefit from low interest rates, given our AAA credit rating.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, the SINGA bonds could potentially extend the Singapore Government Securities (SGS) yield curve beyond its current 30-year maturity depending on investor demand and primary dealers' market making obligations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This helps in deepening the bond market domestically too.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But, Mr Speaker, for the man on the street, beyond the technical terms, there may emerge concerns that with the formation of SINGA, we will be tapping on bond markets and see more foreign exchange exposure for our long-term infrastructure spending.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are valid concerns, especially if there are some level of market exposure and liabilities that may be created.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our finances are strong, with assets well in excess of liabilities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is being demonstrated in the COVID-19 crisis, where the Government could purchase vaccines for the whole population while introducing various financial assistance schemes to help citizens and keep the economy and job market abreast.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Looking ahead, I would like to ask if the Government has considered the plausible worst-case scenarios that would see the Government's balance sheets and net foreign assets being weakened?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What if our capital efficiency advantage weakens as global interest rates rise sharply?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister explained it very clearly and in detailed form in his speech earlier when talking about the 5.5% effective yield-to-maturity rates.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But my question is: has MOF and other economic policy agencies such as MAS done counter-factual simulations using market shock variable?.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But, may I ask the Minister if our debt servicing costs will be funded by our annual Budget and met from our overall revenue?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If so, assuming we have a full $90 billion issuance and we are constrained by our current principle of having an overall balanced Budget over each term of Government, can the Minister share if this will affect our annual fiscal policy options in periods of extreme crisis in the future?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Deputy Prime Minister also share the different phases of fiscal policy options in a crisis or national emergency, for example, if we are to use past reserves first, at the first stage; do we then need to liquidate GIC investments second or do we need to borrow last?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The amount that we are borrowing – up to $90 billion – can be quite significant.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Thirdly, may I ask the Deputy Prime Minister on the SINGA infrastructure bond issuance: what are our baseline economic assumptions and how do we ensure issuance supply is calibrated to market demand?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Following the introduction of SINGA, will the duration of the SGS market change over the medium term?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On a separate issue, some projects were previously placed under Statutory Board issuance but moving forward, will these be funded by the SINGA bonds if they qualify?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is useful to know if the SINGA bond issuance will have a crowding out effect on future bond issuances by Statutory Boards.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Globally, there has been steady growth in sovereign green, social and sustainable, or GSS, bond issuances in the past years.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Looking at the experience of Germany's sovereign green bonds, there might be room for a sustained premium or lower yield to green issues versus conventional issues.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is a forward-looking Bill with Singapore's economic, environmental and social sustainability in mind.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It would appear that the annual interest threshold is set rather high, considering that the coupon rate of a 30-year Temasek bond is only 2.25% per annum.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the Minister elaborate on why the annual interest threshold is set at $5 billion?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Why not $88 billion – an auspicious number?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Has the Government already selected the projects to fund and have their estimated costs in hand?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Otherwise, why not choose a figure which is a percentage of our GDP or a multiple of the average development expenditure for the past three years, for example?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Instead of an aggregate limit of $90 billion, is it possible to consider an annual debt ceiling which is based on the estimated infrastructure expenditure over the next 10 to 15 years?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have seen how costs have ballooned over the past one year and costs will only continue to escalate in the future.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, net short-term debt should not exceed a certain percentage of budgeted expenditure in a financial year.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We can have a separate category for long-term debt.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singapore's institutional framework has often been praised for its high level of quality, predictability and transparency.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Although it was brought up during the Committee of Supply debate in March, I wonder if we could set such prudent debt limits in consultation with our citizens?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I understand that in New Zealand, for example, the government had organised consultative sessions with industry bodies and its citizens to share the need to borrow or issue bonds.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I fully support the decision to issue green bonds to fund environmentally sustainable long-term projects under SINGA.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This will result in a deeper and more varied Singapore bond market, providing more opportunities for long-term investors.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the Government set aside a good portion of SINGA bonds for retail investors?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope a significant portion in affordable denominations can be reserved for Singaporeans so that more of our citizens can own a piece of our country's future development.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With the growing concern and interest in environmental issues globally, we will be able to attract a substantial pool of international green investors.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As what Member Saktiandi Supaat has said, drawing on the experience of Germany's sovereign green bonds, our potential investors should be able to attach a durable premium – in other words, lower yield – to green issues versus the conventional ones.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I understand that many investors who support green initiatives accept lower yields because it is important for them to finance environmentally responsible projects.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With aligned goals for the benefit of our planet, our green issues should do well.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the Minister provide estimates for the various initiatives in our Singapore Green Plan 2030 and fight against climate change which will be supported by the SINGA green bonds, such as the construction of polders and so forth?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can we set out a range of planning instruments relating to the provision of infrastructure?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These can include a 20- to 30-year infrastructure strategy and 10-year plans for services and activities broken down to how they are related to financial strategies and annual plans.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Next, I would like to ask if bond issuance is the only mechanism to fund infrastructure development.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Perhaps we should look into the availability of private partners for public-private partnerships to finance local investments, for example, special purpose vehicles or lease contracts.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope Singapore's sovereign rating remains AAA forever.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, in the event that our rating deteriorates, to limit financial risks, derivative contracts should not be allowed and speculative positions with derivatives should not be permitted.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   The Significant Infrastructure Government Loan Bill will play a vital role in the development of our country's infrastructure construction in the future.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With complete infrastructure and social resources such as sea walls, transportation, hospitals and schools, we can build a beautiful, sustainable and warm home, an ideal home where the capable can be gainfully employed, the young can learn, the sick can be treated and the elderly can find joy.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I would also like to take this opportunity to thank Deputy Prime Minister Heng for his contribution to Singapore in his capacity as Finance Minister.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This will materially improve national productivity and benefit the society and the environment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Additionally, given the substantial drawing of national reserves to finance the costs from the COVID-19 pandemic, SINGA will create extra fiscal space and allow for the debt to be paid back in a manner that is equitable across generations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That said, this is the first time in 40 years that the Government will be borrowing very large sums of money.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is important to have strict and robust safeguards in place to ensure that the borrowing is sustainable and prudent.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have two areas of clarifications on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first area of clarification is on safeguarding the proper use of the loans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Deputy Prime Minister has provided assurances that the Bill includes "strict safeguards on the projects that can qualify for borrowing and the amounts that can be borrowed".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, the definition of "nationally significant infrastructure" laid out in the new section 2(1) can be broadly construed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, can Deputy Prime Minister share what checks and balances will be put in place to assess if the loan is raised for infrastructure projects that are indeed nationally significant?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, while the new section 9 provides the Minister's power to raise a loan is non-delegable, can a committee be formed to deliberate and recommend if a loan should be raised for an infrastructure project?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is equivalent to about two-thirds of total outstanding Singapore Government Securities (SGS).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Deputy Prime Minister share what checks are in place to ensure that the loan is used in a manner that is responsible, prudent and sustainable by the party the loan is issued to?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Thirdly, the Government trusts that Singapore would likely benefit from favourable interest rates given Singapore's AAA credit rating and the current market environment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Low interest rates would keep the intergenerational costs of public debt low.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, in the off-chance that interest rates rise substantially, what contingency plans does the Ministry have in place to finance the debt in a way that does not impose a huge burden on future generations?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second area of clarification is around financing green infrastructure projects.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With SINGA, the Government will issue a new category of government infrastructure bond, termed SGS (Infrastructure).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Green bonds will form a subset of SGS (Infrastructure).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Examples of these standards include the International Capital Market Association (ICMA)'s Green Bond Principles, EU Green Bond Standards and the ASEAN Green Bond Standards.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Taking reference from these "green" standards can be important in giving lenders and financiers assurance and confidence that green financing is true to its label.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If not, can Deputy Prime Minister, together with MSE, consider doing so?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Deputy Prime Minister share if there are plans for climate mitigation projects?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is not only important that we adapt to climate change, but that we work to minimise its impact in the first place.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This index ranked cities by measuring key dimensions, such as economic dynamism, innovation, sustainable environmental policies as well as transportation.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Transportation infrastructure is a new factor included by the researchers this year as they noted it is critical to supporting social mobility, a key feature of great cities.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore will need to continue to invest in its infrastructure for its long-term development to continue to be amongst the top cities in the world for its citizens to live in and be an international place to do business.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I fundamentally agree with this approach as it is also economically efficient given the ability of Singapore to tap the debt markets.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Given the past and continued strong track record of this Government, we have every reason to be confident that the SINGA Bill would be used optimally for the benefit of our citizens.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Notwithstanding this, I am glad that there have been ample safeguards built into this legislation, such as, one, a precise definition of what an "infrastructure project" means to eliminate the possibility of using this Bill as a backdoor way to spend on soft investments; and two, a clear definition of "qualifying capital expenditure" to exclude expenditures, such as the cost of repairs and maintenance which should be rightfully expensed when incurred and therefore not be allowed for capitalisation.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This will ensure that such expenses, including soft investments, will need to be transparently put before this House as part of our annual Budget debate.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: While we are on the topic of safeguards, since significant infrastructure have long development lead times as well as useful life, can the Deputy Prime Minister clarify how will the financial mechanism be applied to decide on the borrowing tenor since most of these public projects are unlikely to have a clear cashflow stream?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister had mentioned that nationally significant infrastructure funding is managed on a bond portfolio approach.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: However, a portfolio is made up of many projects.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The question I have is that, at a project level, for example, if the useful life of the flood defences project is 50 years, can the Government decide to fund this through a shorter borrowing tenor of, say, 10 years?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: If so, when the time comes for rolling over the borrowings, interest rates could have risen potentially, leaving the future term of Government with a higher interest rate expense.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In short, as interest rate trends are not always predictable, the question more broadly is: how will the Government hedge the interest rate risk since we ought to also protect the future generation from shouldering an unexpected debt servicing burden?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This rate appears to be a good and reasonable control in the context of today's low interest rate environment.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: However, I note that 10-year SGS yields were over 5% in the late 1990s.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: If there is a resurgence of inflation, which is not unlikely, given the massive stimulus by governments, such as the US, and a corresponding rise in the level of risk-free rates, it is good that the future Government be required to come back to debate and receive support from this House.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: While this legislation will help address the funding of our significant infrastructure needs, from a financial market development standpoint, the issuance of SINGA bonds will help further deepen Singapore as an international financial market.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Currently, there is lower liquidity at the longer end of the sovereign rate curve given that the Government has had little need to issue longer dated financial instruments.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Additionally, SINGA bonds would be a good asset-liability match for financial institutions such as insurers which have long dated funds that needs to be deployed as the insurance market grows further.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Leader, would you like to move an exempted business Motion?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Notwithstanding the fact that interest rates could continue to be low for a protracted period of time, the risk remains that rates could move higher in the event of a strong economic recovery or even more importantly, a material rise in inflation.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But what is more important than rates per se is perhaps the differential between rates or "r" and growth "g", in other words, "r" minus "g".

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Stated plainly, what matters is whether you can make more than you pay through borrowing.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, I hope that as we envision a portfolio of tenors, we will pay attention to refinancing risks in particular.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, in the end though, the important thing is, our economy must continue to grow.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We must continue to transform the economy, spend on infrastructure, cut waste out of public spending, taking a value-based approach to all that we do.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Some might say tapping the reserves and borrowing are really two sides of the same coin.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Under a strong growth recovery, it should free up more budget for recurrent expenditure, including welfare, healthcare and yes, education and reskilling, for the current generation today, all of which Members from both sides of the House have asked on multiple occasions.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Even though Leader has just extended our time for my speech, I think if I were to go on to every single one of your suggestion, we will be here way past midnight.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, let me just cluster your suggestions around three broad questions.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: First, why is the Government borrowing for nationally significant infrastructure?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Second, is borrowing under SINGA a prudent approach?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And third, how would the Government manage the debt issuance under SINGA?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Before I address these questions, I would first like to thank Mr Liang Eng Hwa for laying out the principles and considerations clearly.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Indeed, as Mr Liang has rightfully pointed out, borrowing should be anchored by our overarching guiding values of prudence, discipline and equity.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In fact, the key reason, as he pointed out, for borrowing is about intergenerational equity, a point which Prof Hoon Hian Teck also made about intergenerational equity or re-distributive justice.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In fact, Prof Hoon mentioned that, for example, on climate change, the building of dykes and polders and other structures for keeping our island safe, is also a responsibility to unborn generations for which the Government is acting on their behalf.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: What we are doing builds on what we have been doing in managing our reserves to make sure that while we draw on our NIRC for our recurrent spending, we are also leaving aside sums for the future generation, so that they too can manage the long term.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, this has been, in fact, the Government's approach which has been a very carefully calibrated one.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, let me now go into some details.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: All these borrowings are invested and are not spent, and the returns on our investments are able to cover the borrowing costs over the long term.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This includes the higher interest rates that we give to CPF members for the monies in their CPF accounts.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We manage our borrowings carefully to ensure that we have the financial resources to repay our debts.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: While we used to borrow for spending in our development years, there has not been a need for us to do so since the 1990s because of strong growth and healthy revenues.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Prudent management of our finances during these good years also helped us to build up our reserves.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Mr Liang pointed out, we could therefore now count on our rainy-day fund to mount a quick and decisive response to protect the lives and livelihoods of Singaporeans when the COVID-19 crisis hit last year.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We did not have to incur a single cent of debt to fund our COVID-19 response.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our approach is different from other countries as our circumstances are different.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Ms Foo Mee Har reminded us, even during the COVID-19 crisis, some countries already had high levels of net government debt as they borrowed to fund recurrent needs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Some of these countries had to borrow even more to fund their COVID-19 response.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: By contrast, Singapore does not have any net debt.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This strong fiscal position puts us in a good position to emerge stronger from the COVID-19 crisis.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, let me address why do we limit it to nationally significant infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This Bill is a continuation of our careful and calibrated approach towards borrowing.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As mentioned in my earlier speech, we are anticipating a hump of development expenditure as we embark on a generational upgrade of nationally significant infrastructure to improve the lives of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Borrowing and capitalisation of nationally significant infrastructure will help us spread out its lumpy costs, to better match the timing of the benefits to the timing of the spending.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have been anticipating this need for quite some time now.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I first announced that we were studying the option of borrowing for nationally significant infrastructure about two years ago in 2019.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I had also at the outset of my speech showed you this infrastructure hump that we are facing.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Several Members have made comments relating about why $90 billion, why not lower it, why not increase it, why the criteria, and so on.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In fact, we are borrowing this $90 billion or we are going to borrow this $90 billion, in order to smooth out the funding needs because of this hump.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Over and above that, our development expenditure will continue.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Several Members, including Mr Liang, have also asked about what is the impact on our AAA credit rating and several Members have pointed that this is the first time that we are borrowing for spending since the 1990s and it is not for a small sum; it is $90 billion.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: MOF and MAS have in fact engaged the three major credit rating agencies – S&P, Moody's and Fitch – to explain our approach on these borrowings.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: They too recognised that our approach is underpinned by key principles of prudence and sustainability.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is because they understand that the Government is committed to a balanced Budget framework and to fund recurrent spending with recurrent revenue.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Having sound macro-policies – fiscal, monetary and structural – is paramount.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Ms Foo Mee Har reminded us, we cannot take our AAA rating for granted.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We must be prudent in how much we borrow and what we use our borrowings for.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Edward Chia, Mr Don Wee and Mr Xie Yao Quan asked about the Government's considerations in setting the project cost threshold at $4 billion and if the Government would review it in future.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As explained earlier, the Government is starting off more prudently by limiting the scope of SINGA to larger projects that tend to have greater intergenerational benefits.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Infrastructure projects are in most instances intended to provide a stream of services over many years, and a diverse set is needed for Singapore and many other countries.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As Mr Don Wee pointed out, the Sports Hub itself, and whether it is Sports Hub or KPE, are all over a billion dollars.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is not our intent that all types of infrastructure will be funded by borrowing.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is not our intent to fund all types of infrastructure by borrowing.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It must eventually be repaid by future taxpayers.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If we borrow for all infrastructure projects, even the smaller ones, we will leave our children to shoulder a bigger stream of debt repayments.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This would not be prudent, especially in view of our maturing economy and slower growth rates.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, the Government will continue to plan for and build a range of infrastructure to meet the needs of our people.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Such development expenditure will remain a part of our annual Budget, to be funded by the recurrent revenues that the Government has to collect.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As to what should count as infrastructure, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim and Mr Louis Chua mentioned a few points and I want to thank Mr Murali Pillai for his thoughtful comments to these suggestions.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Assoc Prof Jamus explained his proposal to expand the scope of borrowing.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, I take it that he is in full support of SINGA to fund large-scale infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But what he wants is an additional bit to further expand the scope of borrowing to include non-infrastructure spending.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And I thank Mr Derrick Goh, who has just spoken, for his warning that we should not dress all types of spending as "soft infrastructure".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In terms of spending on education, healthcare, the Government recognises the importance of spending on these needs but we should always focus on how well we spend, not how much we spend.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And we should always focus on the outcome and effectiveness of our spending, not on how big a sum of money we spend.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, we have made significant investments and ensured good outcomes.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I have shown our effectiveness spending in education and health in this House before and I hope that Members will refer back to the Hansard and the charts that I have shown.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This has been internationally recognised such as the World Bank Human Capital Index.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The second point is that Assoc Prof Jamus has also cited several studies, macro studies, and may not apply to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Singapore has already achieved high levels of schooling especially for our younger cohorts.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our university cohort participation rate is already at 42%, comparable to the advanced economies.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: More importantly, we have high employment and good outcomes.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Louis Chua cited the recent US stimulus package and said it included a whole range of spending on social infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: He then compared with what we are spending and suggested that actually we should be spending more.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: When we are looking at spending, we should be asking ourselves what do we have to spend on, what has been achieved and what other problems are we trying to fix?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, both Assoc Prof Jamus and Mr Louis Chua's comments point to the risk, in fact, a very major risk, that if you do not draw clear lines every time expenditure items come up for debate, you would then blur the lines and the lines will keep getting blurrer.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And you can argue that everything that a country needs to get itself working, to get working, would qualify.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Just coin it by some nice names and call it "soft infrastructure".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: What about healthcare, education, social spending, spending to maintain social cohesion?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Let us stick to what are factors rather than to keep blurring the arguments.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If you want to have higher spending on healthcare, on education, say so, and we can debate whether are we spending enough or not enough.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There is one other very significant point which I would like everyone to bear in mind.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As I have said, borrowing helps you to finance but debt has to be repaid.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The argument is that borrowing for recurrent expenditure will pay for itself because you will get higher returns on human capital versus infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But this has not been borne out anywhere in the world.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In fact, I will talk more about this later.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, if we borrow for one third of our recurrent spending, no matter how cost-effective they are, this would, over time, create a high debt burden for future generations.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I would also like to thank Prof Hoon Hian Teck for pointing out very clearly that we need to have the capacity to raise revenue, and this is critical for fiscal sustainability.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Indeed, the credit worthiness of Singapore, the extent of credit that people are willing to recognise for Singapore and grade Singapore, depends critically on whether they think that we have a sustainable fiscal policy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: That, again, depends on how willing the Government is to maintain financial discipline and to raise taxes where it is necessary.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If we do not do that, what is likely to happen is that your credit ratings will fall, the risk premium will rise.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And this is going to have an effect on the entire economy – on not just Government borrowing but on corporate borrowing, and in turn, this is going to affect the jobs of our people.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Because if we make ourselves a less desirable place for investments, it will come back and haunt us.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai's long speech boils down to actually one argument: that we have a lot of money – more than enough – because our reserves are large and we can just spend and spend and spend.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Then, he comes up with some estimates of how big our reserves are.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As I have said before in this Parliament, we do not comment on the size of our reserves for the reasons I have set out in my earlier speeches.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai also conflated intergenerational equity for long-lived assets with intergenerational equity.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai also claimed that the burden for paying various expenses came down to our workers.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: About half of our workers do not pay income tax at all.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, I hope that if Mr Leong Mun Wai would like to make a contribution to policy-making in this Chamber, please be rigorous.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Come here with fresh insights or new facts.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Please do not reread and reread your old script.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked if we can borrow, say, during a crisis.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There is no one-size-fits-all approach to a crisis.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We need to take into account the nature of a crisis and be prepared to use all the tools at our disposal.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We are fortunate to have built up our reserves, which serve, among others, as a rainy day fund – as Mr Liang Eng Hwa pointed out earlier – which we can tap on in times of crisis.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If the global economic outlook worsens unexpectedly, we may have to take exceptional measures.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If we have to draw on past reserves again to support our economy, we may consider raising cash by borrowing.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Doing so would allow our assets to stay invested for the long term.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But as I have said, we will be prepared to use all tools at our disposal but we have to consider this carefully.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa also asked about the update on his suggestion which he raised earlier during the Budget debate – other than SINGA, should we be prepared to borrow to finance investments that allow Singapore to emerge stronger?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Indeed, COVID-19 has accelerated structural changes in the global economy and has disrupted industries and reshaped jobs in significant ways.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We are fortunate that five years ago, we started on our industry transformation and we have achieved results.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In the midst of the crisis, we set up the Emerging Stronger Taskforce to look at how Singapore can emerge stronger from the crisis.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Emerging Stronger Taskforce will be putting out its final report soon.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: There are many good suggestions in the report on how we can build capacity in our companies and in our people so that we can seize opportunities and emerge stronger.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I will study this report carefully and discuss with MOF later on how we can fund additional investments during this period.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is an important opportunity for us to do so.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But if we do borrow for this purpose of emerging stronger, we must set some conditions; set safeguards, as Ms Foo Mee Har reminded us.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is not to become a recurrent fiscal tool.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is important that we must maintain this intergenerational equity.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Ms Foo Mee Har, Mr Louis Ng, Mr Edward Chia and Ms Mariam Jaffar have asked about the checks and balances we need to put in place to ensure that the criteria for nationally significant infrastructure are met and borrowings are well used.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This includes an evaluation through the Gateway Process and a certification by each agency's accounting officer that the criteria in SINGA are met.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: First, all development projects will have to go through the Gateway Process to ensure project worthiness and cost effectiveness before construction – no different from today.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Under the Gateway Process, these projects will first undergo review by MOF as well as the Development Projects Advisory Panel, or DPAP.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The DPAP includes independent third parties, such as academics and industry practitioners, with deep technical expertise.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: They ensure that the project meets Singapore's needs and not only today's needs, as Mr Edward Chia reminded us, but also tomorrow's.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: They also ensure that cost estimates are rigorous and reasonable.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In fact, over the last few years, these processes have led to design improvements and generated savings of several billion dollars in total.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Thereafter, these projects will be subject to further approval by the Ministerial-level Development Planning Committee.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked about the approval process and so did Mr Louis Ng.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Xie Yao Quan suggested that, for prudence, perhaps we should reduce the total borrowing and reduce the interest cost.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But I want to assure Members that Parliament will continue to play an important role to ensure that our infrastructure investments are worthwhile.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: All infrastructure to be financed by borrowings will form part of our development expenditures to be approved through the annual Budget process.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Parliament may carefully scrutinise our proposed infrastructure plans before we proceed with spending and capitalising the development expenditures.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And any Committee of Supply Bill passed by Parliament has to be assented to by the elected President.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: First, I will address the limits on the amount of borrowings that can be raised before addressing the safeguards on the capitalisation of nationally significant infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: SINGA has two key safeguards to limit the amount of borrowings raised.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is equivalent to about four Downtown Lines and about 20% of our GDP in 2020, at current market prices.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Nevertheless, 20% of GDP is lower than the previous borrowing limits under the six Development Loan Acts, or DLAs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: They averaged around 40% of GDP in the year the DLA was introduced.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is also lower than the borrowing limits in other countries.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Some Members, including Mr Don Wee, have asked why use an absolute limit of $90 billion instead, say, of rolling annual limits that are pegged to a percentage of GDP?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: An absolute limit gives certainty to both current and future terms of Government on the amount that they can borrow to spend on nationally significant infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If we peg the limit to GDP, the limit will fluctuate as the size of the economy fluctuates over time.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This will mean a lower limit during an economic downturn, like now, and constrain us from building critical infrastructure at a time when the conditions are right and could help to support the economy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: When we consider nationally significant infrastructure, we must take a longer term view.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Nonetheless, I would like to assure Members, including Mr Edward Chia, Ms Foo Mee Har and Mr Louis Chua, that this $90 billion limit has taken into account future economic growth and expected inflation on the underlying development expenditures.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: On the annual effective interest cost threshold of $5 billion, Mr Xie Yao Quan and Mr Don Wee asked about the considerations behind this threshold and whether it should be lower, given the low interest rates today.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This keeps the level of our interest payments sustainable and this is lower than the borrowing cost in other countries.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For example, interest payment to GDP in the UK in FY2019/2020 is about 1.7%.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Xie and Mr Wee are right that in the current low interest rate environment, we do not expect our interest costs to be near the $5 billion threshold even if we borrow up to the full $90 billion.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But the $5 billion cap provides some buffer when the interest rate cycle turns.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And as several Members have pointed out, interest rates at some point will rise.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, we cannot expect interest rates to remain at current low levels forever and do not forget that this borrowing is not for the next year.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This borrowing is for the coming 15 years.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, I hope this will address Members' suggestion as to whether we should borrow more to take advantage of low interest rates.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Let us remind ourselves that our own interest rates are especially subject to global interest rate volatility, because our capital markets are open and monetary policy is centred on managing the exchange rate.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And there were periods over the last 25 years of our history when our interest rates were much higher.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, what will happen if interest rates rise?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If we borrow too much from the onset, in particular for non-infrastructure expenditure, then we will have a much higher debt ceiling burden when we need to refinance our existing debts and our fiscal situation can spiral downward quickly.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This usually happens in a crisis, when we can least afford it.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But if we borrow prudently to finance only critical, long-term infrastructure that bring significant benefits to Singapore, we can continue to ensure investor confidence even in a high interest rate environment.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This will enable us to retain our triple A credit rating, which can anchor our interest costs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In addition, because we are borrowing for infrastructure where the payment structure typically stretches across time, borrowing costs under SINGA would be averaged out.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, our prudent approach can therefore help us to maintain a strong fiscal position and continue borrowing to finance critical investments, even if interest rate cycles turn upwards.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The interest cost threshold will keep the overall debt servicing costs in check.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Edward Chia and Ms Foo Mee Har asked in the event that we are nearing the interest cost threshold, do we need to raise revenues or divest our financial assets to raise liquidity to repay some of the outstanding borrowings so as to keep within the threshold.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: First, the cap on interest is on the outstanding debt.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Second, the cap is on the effective cost across all the outstanding debt.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is precisely why we need this safeguard to ensure that the Government will continue to exercise care in managing debt and debt servicing for future generations.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If interest costs rises beyond the threshold and we cannot borrow more, the government of the day can re-consider the threshold and debate in Parliament again.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I should also clarify that for outstanding loans, the Government can continue to maintain these borrowings until maturity and not have to repay the outstanding borrowings under SINGA immediately.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Some Members have also asked whether we should borrow the full $90 billion in advance, given the current low interest rates environment.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Indeed, we are prepared to start borrowing for the infrastructure projects that have undergone the rigorous evaluation and review, for which approval has been given for works to begin within the next few years.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This will enable us to benefit from the current low interest rates today and to better spread out the lumpy costs of our major infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But we will not borrow for infrastructure plans that have yet to undergo evaluation and are not firm.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Interest cost is not the only consideration – we have to continue to scrutinise projects rigorously.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And by pacing our borrowings, it will also enable our financial markets to invest in a regular and stable way.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Ms Foo Mee Har and Mr Edward Chia asked about the safeguards.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Besides limiting the amount of borrowings, the safeguards on the capitalisation and depreciation of nationally significant infrastructure assets.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We intend to depreciate the assets evenly via a straight-line depreciation method.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This will ensure that each generation contributes an equal share towards the nationally significant infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This reduces the risk of future generations having to pay for an infrastructure that is becoming functionally obsolete towards the tail end of its useful life.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In addition, Mr Murali Pillai asked about potential abandonment of SINGA projects after borrowings have been raised.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I should first clarify that even the Government has started borrowing for and constructing a project, it has no incentive to abandon any meritorious projects.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Because doing so comes with both tangible costs such as demolition costs that would be charged to the term of the government that abandons the project, as well as intangible costs such as reputational costs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But as Mr Murali Pillai pointed out, there may be other scenarios where projects may be abandoned; for instance, if there is a change a government.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If the new government abandons the project, it would indeed have to pay for the abortive costs, including contracts that have been signed.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: A few months ago, the Malaysian government decided not to proceed with the HSR project and compensated Singapore for the abortive costs in line with our bilateral agreement.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, indeed, there is always a risk that any infrastructural projects, not just the ones that are financed by SINGA borrowings, may be aborted, due to circumstances beyond the Government’s control.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And this is where we have to do our best, to put in place the measures to minimise the risks, and should these risks materialise, to have proper recourse and maintain investors’ confidence in the ability of the Singapore Government to manage the country’s finances properly and observe the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) as the Government’s agent will be issuing a new category of Singapore Government Securities (SGS) under SINGA.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: To delineate this from the existing SGS issued under the GSA, we will rename the SGS issued under the GSA as SGS (Market Development).

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Both categories of SGS will rank pari passu and will be priced along the same yield curve.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: They will also be subject to the same tax and regulatory treatments and will be made available to both institutional and retail investors.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Hence, investors would see both SGS (Infrastructure) and SGS (Market Development) as equivalent substitutes.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: To keep overall issuance costs well anchored, both categories of SGS will be managed holistically, as Mr Saktiandi Supaat pointed out.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This ensures that the overall supply of the SGS will be calibrated to market demand.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: To assess the demand for SGS each year, MAS will consider the prevailing global and domestic financial and monetary conditions, feedback from investors and the infrastructure spending needs under SINGA.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In a year, when more SGS (Infrastructure) need to be issued, MAS will accordingly reduce the issuance of SGS (Market Development), assuming market demand is constant.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Like SGS (Market Development), SGS (Infrastructure) will be issued across a range of tenors.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This will help to manage the overall borrowing costs across the entire yield curve.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The tenors and the overall duration of SGS (Infrastructure) would be calibrated to account for demand from investors.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: When market conditions are supportive, MAS will tilt the tenors for SGS (Infrastructure) towards the longer dated tenors, given that the borrowings are intended to finance infrastructure with long useful lives.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Presently, the longest tenor for SGS is 30 years.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We will consider issuing beyond the 30-year tenor, if there is strong market demand.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Some Members, such as Mr Don Wee and Ms Foo Mee Har, also asked if we will consider issuing SGS denominated in foreign currency.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We will not be issuing such SGS for a start.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: However, the SINGA provides the flexibility to issue SGS denominated in foreign currency.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Together with MAS, the Government will work with the market to explore the possibilities of structuring borrowings differently over time, including SGS denominated in foreign currency, if there is demand.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Should we issue such SGS in the future, we will carefully study the options to mitigate foreign exchange risk, as some Members have pointed out.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: To Mr Saktiandi Supaat’s, Mr Louis Ng’s and Mr Don Wee’s query on green bonds, we will issue Green SGS (Infrastructure) for projects that meet the green criteria.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As announced at Budget 2021, the Government will take the lead in issuing green bonds on selected public infrastructure projects.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: These green bonds are an important enabler of the Singapore Green Plan 2030.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This comprises borrowings by both the Government under SINGA as well as borrowings by the Statutory Boards.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Preliminarily, Second Party Opinion providers, which are institutions with environmental expertise to provide independent opinion on Green Bond Frameworks, have indicated that our MRT projects are likely to qualify for green issuances under SINGA, as electric passenger rail is the greenest mode of mass transportation.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Government is working with MAS and industry partners to establish our own Green Bond Frameworks for Green SGS (Infrastructure), taking reference from international standards, as highlighted by Mr Louis Ng.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As we are only just starting out our green bond programme, we will not be stipulating a minimum percentage of green bonds under SINGA for now.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Nonetheless, we thank Mr Murali Pillai for his suggestion.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As for green bonds issued by Statutory Boards, we expect NEA to issue green bonds for the Tuas Nexus project.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Ms Foo Mee Har also asked how borrowings under SINGA will interact with existing borrowings by Statutory Boards.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: To reiterate, borrowings under SINGA will be used to finance an upcoming generational upgrade of infrastructure which are large-scale projects which can cost up to tens of billions of dollars.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: While our Statutory boards do currently borrow for infrastructure; it would be more capital efficient for such large-scale borrowings to be undertaken on Government’s balance sheet to optimise financing costs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Nonetheless, there is still a place for borrowings by Statutory Boards.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We expect Statutory Boards to continue issuing bonds, including green bonds, to finance smaller scale infrastructure that do not fall within the scope of SINGA.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, let me sum up by situating borrowing under the SINGA within our broader fiscal strategy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And in so doing, address Members’ questions about our fiscal approach.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our fiscal strategy must remain true to our core values of prudence and stewardship.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But it must also be resilient and nimble to adapting to changing times.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Hence, we have employed a differentiated fiscal strategy for different kinds of expenditure.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For infrastructure needs, we will now employ borrowing as one of our financing strategies.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And this is in addition to other financing strategies such as pre-saving in the Rail Infrastructure Fund and the Coastal and Flood Protection Fund.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Where appropriate, we will also consider ways to partner the private sector, as suggested by Mr Don Wee and several others, to fund infrastructure such as electrical grid upgrades to support electric vehicle charging infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: SINGA allows us to borrow to finance nationally significant infrastructure in a prudent and disciplined way.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The safeguards help to ensure that the costs of borrowing remain sustainable and that these costs can be met by overall revenues without constraining our ability to pay for future needs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We will also continue to remain in a net asset position.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The majority of the Government borrowings will continue to be issued under the existing LTBA and GSA for non-spending purposes.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As for recurrent spending, such as healthcare and social spending, it is more sustainable to meet these growing needs through revenue that we can collect on an on-going basis, such as taxes.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Borrowing is not revenue, let me repeat that, and it must eventually be repaid by future taxpayers.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Such recurrent spending is in addition to our nationally significant infrastructure needs, which we will be financing through borrowings under SINGA.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Without borrowing, we might have needed to raise taxes even more in the next few years to fund the large upfront costs of these infrastructure, as Ms Foo Mee Har highlighted.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, borrowing helps us to spread the costs of infrastructure over generations and avoid steep increases in taxes over the coming years.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: First, the details of how our capitalisation under SINGA will be allowed.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I have mentioned that earlier on in my main speech.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Second, does the $90 billion limit take into account upgrading and maintenance cost of the infrastructure over the lifetime of infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, put it another way, this is the amount of taxes we would have needed to raise have we not implemented SINGA, or the amount of spending that we will have to cut or not spend on SINGA.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, to conclude, Mr Speaker, Sir, as we emerge from COVID-19, we must continue to build a better Singapore for the future.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But we must remain prudent even as we do so and maintain our strong fiscal position.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And to quote Ms Foo again, "the debt we accumulate must not put unfair pressure on future generations." Borrowing for nationally significant infrastructure under SINGA will help us to achieve these goals and set Singapore up for future success.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I have four questions to clarify for the Deputy Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I am very perturbed by his saying that I am not contributing to this Parliament.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I do not take umbrage because I aim to be a gentleman, but I am seriously perturbed.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I think what I am trying to do here is to complete the picture.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I think maybe because of the various commitment of Government, some of the information that is coming out of this Parliament is not complete.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Three, you provided some figures to say that middle class Singaporeans are getting more from the Government than the taxes they pay.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It is a very serious matter, you know.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: If we have that much resources, we almost have 7% to 8% of our GDP, including when you take into consideration the land sales and the NIR we have.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Every year, we have about 7% to 8% of our GDP in this sort of resources.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And you tell me that going forward, our expenditures will still be more than this.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Then, we have to look at our expenditures very carefully.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Those are the four questions, Deputy Prime Minster, please.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: First, I thank Mr Leong Mun Wai for the questions.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I did not say that you are not contributing to this Parliament.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I said, "Please be rigorous when you come to Parliament and justify your position".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: You asked four specific questions so you should not be perturbed nor should you take umbrage.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It now constitutes 3% of GDP of our expenditure – huge amount!

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: More than any single category of taxes, whether it is GST, personal income tax or corporate income taxes.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And we are only using 50% because it is our responsibility to put back that 50% for future generations as our needs grow.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If our parliamentarians have taken the approach that you have advocated, we will not even be debating this because we will just be talking about how much debt to issue in order to fund.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And my numbers which I have quoted, on many of the OECD countries, that the average is 80% of the debt to GDP and how that has increased further.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And second, you have asked me to confirm whether reserves in the gross financial statements are correct.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Well, the statements are prepared and are correct when we publish it, but whether this can be spent is a separate matter.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The third question is, to ask me to go to my constituents and make the claim that the more taxes you pay, the more benefit you get.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I do not know your logic because I did not, in any way, say that the more taxes you pay, the more benefits you get.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Again, since you entered Parliament, in the various Budget debates, you have been raising this.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I have been answering as patiently as I can.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I hope that this will be the last time that I have to answer this.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: You have to see GST in the context of the entire expenditure of our households; and on what taxes they pay and what rebates they get.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And again, all my numbers, I stand by all the numbers I have used in my past parliamentary speeches.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, please do your homework and check it out.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And finally, you asked me: am I prepared to prepare 20-year expenditure forecast of all that is to come?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Because just two years ago, I would not have predicted that we would have faced such a generational crisis that I had to go to the President to touch our past reserves, to unlock our past reserves for them to be used, and $53.7 billion is not a small sum.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So any projection, if anybody claims to have the foresight to project 20 years, I would say, better not trust that person.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Even five years, I cannot tell you what exactly will happen.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We can project how much our healthcare costs will be going up because it is our responsibility to provide for that.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We know globally what is the trend of how ageing affects healthcare costs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: What we do not know is what new treatments will come out, how lifespan will continue to grow, what kind of new drugs, new treatments, approaches will come and therefore, how healthcare expenditure will rise.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, even whatever numbers that Minister Gan Kim Yong and I have been working on, we are always conscious that this represents, in a way, a lower limit, we have to provide at least for that amount.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And for you to argue that we have 7% to 8% of GDP, equals NIRC, equals to land sales – your numbers are just completely off.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, I hope that you take your parliamentary duties seriously and that you do your homework before you come and debates with us on the numbers.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, I have not called you yet.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Sorry, I have to interject because there were a lot of allegations.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai, if you have fresh insights, please.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: All the numbers that I am saying are backed by research.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, what the Deputy Prime Minister has said just now, can I confirm again that you agreed that: first, we have $128 billion of fiscal resources this year but you define and classify some of it into revenue, and some not into revenue.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, the Government is doing a different classification from what we see as total resources available.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, can I suggest we cover new grounds?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I think whatever Deputy Prime Minister has explained, he has explained.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If you are holding your position, you are free to do so but if we can have new insights; otherwise, we can move on.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: What the Deputy Prime Minister is saying is – whatever he says is fact.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Whatever we present as an alternative view is something that can be brushed off and I have to go back and do more homework and be more rigorous.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: That is, I do not want to take offence.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Something that I take—I think that is not professional.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, you will have a position in which you disagree with the Deputy Prime Minister and we can recognise that.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, do you have new insights that you would like to share with us in Parliament, apart from going over the same ground?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The Deputy Prime Minister said that he could provide the recurrent expenditures as expected over the next 10 to 20 years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: If I may request that he provides us with that so that we can scrutinise —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, the Deputy Prime Minister has replied as to how he wants to approach that.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: There is no point repeating the same question because you will get the same answer.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Deputy Prime Minister has replied and said that he is not able to provide the projection for the next 20 years because it is hard to project what the future will be.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But he did say that recurrent expenditures are possible.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Some expenditures, like the COVID-19 expenditures and all that, of course, are not predictable.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, I am requesting whether he can provide those that are possible.

speaker: Mr Speaker
