text: Would the Deputy Prime Minister like to respond to any of that?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I hope that you were not insinuating that I was non-professional in my approach.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Because, if that were so, then I am completely speechless.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We had gone through the Global Financial Crisis, the Asian Financial Crisis and SARS.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, crises are a recurrent feature of our life today and for us to pretend that we have the foresight to see clearly what will happen in the future is just not right.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As I said, even then, in my many meetings with Minister Gan Kim Yong, our Health Minister, we had gone through our projections over and over again, and the numbers keep changing because of the factors that I mentioned in my speech earlier.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, I hope that the Member listens carefully and not just look at the phone, please.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I am speaking and the Member is just looking at the phone.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I hope the Member has the courtesy to at least listen when I am trying so hard to address the points, even though I am not obliged to stand up and answer.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, if you could let the Deputy Prime Minister finish.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The IMF provides for a range of ways in which certain expenditures can be counted or not counted, because the structures of governments in different countries are different.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: They have national government, they have state governments, they have city governments.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: What constitutes public spending will all have to be aggregated properly, in order to make useful comparison.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In Singapore's case, we have made it very clear – including during our IMF consultations – that we abide by these standards.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have always taken the same standards and reported our numbers consistently as to what we can spend and what we cannot spend.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, please do not confuse the public that the Government arbitrarily decides on what can be spent and what cannot be spent.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is a very serious allegation which I hope you will take back.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Deputy Prime Minister, I would like to clarify again.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I do not think the definitions of NIR or NIRC, all these are IMF definitions.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Leong, of course, they are not IMF definitions because which country in the world has NIRC?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Then, inside the Budget and financial statements, there is a table of total receipts, and inside that, it includes what we call cash flow.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: If we use the cash flow, the Budget deficit will also not be so big.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Mr Leong, I do not want to waste Members' time on this.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And I hope that every one of us in this House and in Singapore will abide by that principle and will understand the need for us to remain prudent and that we are a tiny red dot with no natural resources and for which we are subject to the vagaries of the global economy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We are an extremely open economy as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I have just two clarification questions that I hope will be a little tamer in nature.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: My first has to do with the purpose of investment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: A point was raised, both by Member Saktiandi Supaat as well as Minister Heng, that we are already number one globally on the Human Development Index.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But, of course, we are debating infrastructure borrowing and our infrastructure ranking, incidentally, according to the World Economic Forum, is also number one.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, the first clarification is, surely, we do not invest only on the basis of the past or where we are now.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Surely, we want to invest for where we want to be.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The second point that Minster Heng mentioned was that we should not count all education and health expenditures as infrastructure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: That is why I did not just wave my hands and suggest some random expenditures in these areas.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I specifically spent one whole page of my speech explaining specific conditions where human capital projects would actually qualify as soft infrastructure.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Suggestions I made would all pay for themselves and, just as important, satisfy intergenerational equity, a point that has been repeatedly made in this House over the course of this debate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, I wonder whether the Minister will consider any form of soft infrastructure that satisfies clear conditions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Or are these always going to be off the table?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: First, on the point that we are number one in the world based on the Human Development Index and, for infrastructure, we are also number one, so, do we need to invest in infrastructure?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The answer is, of course, yes, because the Member supported the infrastructure Bill as well.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But as to whether do we, therefore, need to invest further in human capital development – absolutely, which is why I said that, on healthcare, I had so many discussions with Minister Gan Kim Yong on healthcare expenditure and why we need to continue to provide for healthcare expenditure.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Whether you call it “investments”, whether you call it by any other name, the fact is we do need to spend more on healthcare to take better care of our ageing population.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: When I was in MOE, we were already building on the investments that were made by previous Education Ministers, including Senior Minister Teo Chee Hean, and, over the years, we have been adding to our investments in education.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, it is not as if that the Government has stopped investing in education.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: So, please remember, as I said in my Budget Statements before, do not take every Budget as a standalone Budget.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Every Budget builds on past Budgets and, therefore, we have to look at the cumulative effects of all these spending, investments and the outcomes that they have achieved.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: On the Member's second point about whether I would ever consider any form of soft infrastructure and the Member said that he has spent a whole page specifying the conditions under which they would qualify.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I looked at the spending patterns of various countries and one education minister – whom I shall not name – said to me, "Why are you coming to study us?" And I said, "Well, because you have great peaks of excellence".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And he said, "Yes, but we have very deep valleys as well".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And I explained we will study from the best and look at how best we can learn, and we learn from each other.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And I have seen so many proposals on why spending more in this area or that area would make a bigger impact.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The fact is that you have to consider education holistically.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is not just what you spend on pre-school, Primary school, Secondary school or University.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is important for us to be rigorous about it, make out the case as to which are the areas of education spending which are lacking and what exactly would we do.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And do not get onto the wrong path, because I have also studied systems which had extremely high subsidies for students at various levels.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We awfully regret that decision because, now, it is impossible for us to take back".

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The Member is an Associate Professor of Economics and Finance, and I think the Member would understand these arguments quite well.
